items.stem: A community nurse teaches a neighbourhood group how to reduce West Nile virus risk. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an Environmental Protection Agency–registered insect repellent when outdoors during mosquito season.
Wear long, loose-fitting shirts and pants to reduce skin exposure to mosquito bites.
Avoid outdoor exposure between dusk and dawn when West Nile–carrying mosquitoes are most active, when possible.
Rely on a licensed human West Nile vaccine as the primary prevention strategy for everyone.
Use window and door screens or air conditioning to keep mosquitoes outside the home.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: use EPA-registered insect repellent. Merck: personal protective measures including DEET-type repellents.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC: wear long, loose-fitting shirts and pants. Merck: protective attire to decrease mosquito exposure.
rationales.C: Correct. CDC: avoid being outside between dusk and dawn when mosquitoes that spread West Nile are most active.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC and Merck: no licensed West Nile vaccines are available for use in humans.
rationales.E: Correct. CDC: use screens on windows and doors or air conditioning to keep mosquitoes outside.

items.stem: A home-care nurse reviews hot-weather safety with an older adult who lives alone. For each teaching point, select Accurate or Not accurate.

rows.text: Stay in air-conditioned spaces as much as possible; use cooling centres or other cool public places if home has no air conditioning
Rely on a household fan alone as the main cooling method when outdoor temperatures are extremely high
Drink more water than usual and do not wait until thirst appears (unless a clinician has limited fluids)
Wear loose, lightweight, light-coloured clothing outdoors in the heat

rationales.R1: Accurate. CDC (older adults): stay in air-conditioned buildings; locate cooling shelters if needed. Merck: older adults should not remain in unventilated residences without air-conditioning in excessive heat.
rationales.R2: Not accurate. CDC: do not rely on a fan as the main cooling source when it is really hot. Merck emphasizes environmental modification and air-conditioning for older adults.
rationales.R3: Accurate. CDC: drink more water than usual and do not wait until thirsty; ask clinician if fluids are limited. Merck: maintain adequate hydration.
rationales.R4: Accurate. CDC: wear loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing. Merck: wear light, loose-fitting clothing.

items.stem: An outdoor worker is brought to triage after collapsing on a hot day. Which finding cluster best supports heatstroke rather than heat exhaustion?

options.text: Core temperature greater than 40 °C with altered mental status (confusion, delirium, or coma)
Mild fatigue with intact mental status and temperature clearly below 40 °C
Isolated muscle cramps after exercise with a normal neurologic examination
Afebrile seasonal rhinitis without heat exposure history

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: heatstroke is differentiated by CNS dysfunction and temperature > 40 °C; hallmark is CNS dysfunction with core temperature > 40 °C.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck: heat exhaustion lacks the heatstroke defining pair of CNS dysfunction with temperature > 40 °C (heat exhaustion has intact CNS and usually lower temperature).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Isolated cramps without CNS dysfunction/high core temperature are not heatstroke (Merck; CDC describes heat stroke as more severe progression).

items.stem: A runner collapses after a long race on a humid day. Rectal temperature is 41.2 °C and the client is confused and combative. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, 2 priority actions, and 2 parameters that support heatstroke.

conditions.text: Heatstroke with hyperthermia and CNS dysfunction
Isolated heat cramps without systemic illness

actions.text: Begin rapid aggressive cooling (cold-water immersion when available, or evaporative cooling) and arrange urgent transport/hospital care
Delay cooling until laboratory confirmation of a rare pathogen
Provide only oral fluids and observe outdoors in full sun without cooling
Support airway/circulation as needed and give intravenous fluid/electrolyte replacement while cooling
Apply heavy insulating blankets to raise core temperature further

parameters.text: Normal mentation with temperature clearly under 39 °C
Comfortable rest in a cool room with no symptoms

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Heat exhaustion has intact CNS and usually lower temperature (Merck).
rationales.K2: Correct. Heatstroke: hyperthermia with systemic inflammatory response and CNS dysfunction; temp >40 °C (Merck).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Cramps alone are not heatstroke (Merck overview).
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Mild dehydration without CNS/temp criteria is not heatstroke.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: rapid aggressive cooling is essential; cold-water immersion preferred when available; evaporative cooling also effective; transport/hospital care.
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Cooling must not wait for unrelated lab pathogen workups (Merck emphasizes rapid cooling).
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Leaving the client in sun without cooling worsens heatstroke (Merck/CDC cool and hydrate principles).
rationales.A4: Correct. Merck treatment includes IV fluid/electrolyte replacement and supportive care with cooling.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Goal is rapid cooling, not further heating (Merck).
rationales.P2: Correct. CNS dysfunction is the hallmark (Merck).
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Intact mentation and lower temp fit exhaustion, not stroke (Merck).

items.stem: During a busy shift, a client's condition changes and the current care plan is no longer working. Which TeamSTEPPS leadership action best fits this moment?

options.text: Convene a huddle to communicate adjustments to the plan, update situational awareness, and realign the team
Wait until the next scheduled annual performance appraisal to discuss the change
Avoid telling teammates so each person can invent a separate plan
Delete the prior brief from the record and never revisit goals

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: a huddle monitors/modifies an existing plan when patient condition, team membership, or plan effectiveness changes; any team member can convene. PSNet: huddles share information and raise safety concerns.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Huddles are timely ad-hoc/shift tools, not annual appraisals (AHRQ).
rationales.C: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS requires shared updated plans so the team knows the current care approach (AHRQ).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Briefs/huddles/debriefs support ongoing plan communication; deleting plans without team update is unsafe (AHRQ).

items.stem: A client with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) reports intrusive memories and hypervigilance. Which nursing priority best aligns with evidence-based initial support?

options.text: Help establish personal safety and a supportive environment, then facilitate access to trauma-focused psychotherapy and coordinated care
Argue that the traumatic event never happened until the client agrees
Encourage heavy daily alcohol use to suppress all memories
Isolate the client from all family and community contact permanently

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: treatment includes trauma-focused CBT; self-care begins with personal safety and healthy routines. OpenStax: nurses provide a safe supportive environment, education, self-care strategies, and referrals to psychotherapy/medication.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Do not invalidate trauma; OpenStax/Merck emphasize supportive processing and evidence-based therapy, not denial.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck: intoxicating substances such as alcohol should be used sparingly if at all after trauma.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck: maintain schedule and social engagement when possible; OpenStax supports coordinated supportive care, not permanent isolation.

items.stem: A nurse teaches sleep hygiene to a client with mild insomnia. Complete the statements.

ngn.template: Clients should keep a {B1} and avoid compensating with frequent irregular daytime naps that fragment night sleep. Before bedtime, they should {B2}.

B1.text: highly irregular sleep–wake schedule every day
consistent sleep–wake schedule, especially a regular wake time
pattern of sleeping only after large caffeine loads

B2.text: increase late-evening caffeine, alcohol, and bright screen use
limit caffeine/alcohol near bedtime and reduce stimulating electronics/bright blue light
start vigorous high-intensity exercise immediately before lights out every night
watch the clock continuously and remain in bed for hours while fully awake without stimulus control

rationales.B1a: Incorrect. Irregular schedules impair sleep (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.B1b: Correct. Merck: regular awakening time; avoid naps that fragment nocturnal sleep. OpenStax: maintain a consistent sleep schedule.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Excessive time in bed is not recommended sleep hygiene (Merck approach/table).
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Caffeine near bedtime worsens sleep (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.B2a: Incorrect. Avoid caffeine/alcohol and stimulating screens near bedtime (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.B2b: Correct. Merck inadequate sleep hygiene lists caffeine/stimulants and late excitement; OpenStax advises limiting caffeine/alcohol before bed and avoiding electronics.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Late vigorous exercise/excitement can impair sleep onset (Merck).
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Stimulus control and avoiding clock-watching are preferred (Merck sleep hygiene).

items.stem: A high-risk older adult presents on day 1 of influenza-like illness. The provider plans antiviral therapy. Which teaching point is most accurate?

options.text: Antivirals work best when started early—ideally within about 1 to 2 days after symptom onset
Antibiotics are first-line therapy for uncomplicated influenza virus infection
Antivirals only help if started after two full weeks of untreated fever
No influenza antiviral medicines exist for any patient group

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: antivirals work best when started early, ideally within two days of symptom onset. Merck: antivirals given within 1 to 2 days of onset decrease fever duration and severity.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC: antibiotics do not treat viruses such as influenza. Merck: antibiotics only for complicating bacterial infection.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Benefit is greatest with early start within 1–2 days (CDC; Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neuraminidase inhibitors and other antivirals are available (Merck; CDC).

items.stem: A clinic nurse counsels an older adult about reducing risk of serious pneumococcal disease and community-acquired pneumonia. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Pneumococcal vaccination helps protect against serious pneumococcal infection; influenza vaccination also helps prevent some pneumonias
No vaccines exist that reduce risk of any form of community-acquired pneumonia
Only infants ever benefit from pneumococcal vaccination; adults never do
Pneumococcal disease is never serious in older adults

rationales.A: Correct. Merck CAP Prevention lists pneumococcal and influenza vaccines among vaccines that prevent some forms of CAP. CDC: pneumococcal vaccines protect against serious pneumococcal infections; older adults are at greatest risk of serious illness and death.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck lists several vaccines that prevent some forms of CAP.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for adults based on age/risk as well as children.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: older adults are at greatest risk of serious illness and death from pneumococcal disease.

items.stem: A client presents after a possible bat exposure with a small puncture wound. Which immediate actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water right away
Seek urgent public health/medical assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (vaccine ± rabies immune globulin as indicated)
Ignore wildlife exposures because human rabies never requires prophylaxis
Report the animal type and circumstances to the healthcare/public health team assessing exposure risk
Delay all wound cleaning for several days to 'seal in' any virus

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: wash wounds immediately with soap and water (flush). Merck: cleanse immediately and thoroughly with soap and water.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC: PEP includes wound washing, rabies immune globulin, and vaccine as indicated; seek care urgently. Merck: prompt PEP almost always prevents human rabies; bat contact is an absolute indication for PEP.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: exposures can require urgent PEP assessment; bat contact is high concern.
rationales.D: Correct. CDC: tell clinicians the animal type and abnormal behaviour; assessment depends on animal/circumstances (Merck table).
rationales.E: Incorrect. Immediate cleaning is required; delaying cleaning is opposite of CDC/Merck guidance.

items.stem: An older adult with limited mobility asks how to stay safer during a heat wave at home. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Use air conditioning or visit a cooling centre; avoid relying on a fan alone when it is extremely hot, and drink fluids as advised
Cook large meals with the oven all afternoon to 'dry out' the apartment air
Stop all prescribed medicines without contacting the clinician because heat always cancels prescriptions
Wear heavy dark layered clothing outdoors at midday to trap heat intentionally

rationales.A: Correct. CDC older-adult guidance: prioritize air-conditioned spaces/cooling shelters; do not rely on a fan alone when really hot; drink more water unless clinician limits fluids. Merck: older adults should not remain without air-conditioning in excessive heat; maintain hydration.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC: avoid using the stove/oven because it heats the home.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC: do not stop or change medicines until talking with a clinician.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: wear loose, lightweight, light-coloured clothing.

items.stem: A public health nurse prepares heat-wave messaging for the community. Which prevention messages are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Schedule outdoor activity for cooler parts of the day when possible and take shade breaks
Drink fluids regularly; limit excess alcohol and very sugary drinks during extreme heat
Check on older neighbours and people who live alone during heat waves
Leave infants and older adults in closed parked cars during midday heat to 'acclimatize'
Wear light, loose-fitting clothing outdoors in hot weather

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: do outdoor activities during coolest parts of day; stay in shade; take breaks. Merck: rest breaks in shade; modify environment.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC: stay hydrated; limit sugary, caffeinated, and alcoholic drinks. Merck: maintain adequate hydration.
rationales.C: Correct. CDC: check on family, friends, and neighbours, especially those who live alone or have chronic illness; older adults are high risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck: older adults and children must not be left in automobiles in the hot sun. CDC identifies infants and older adults as high risk.
rationales.E: Correct. CDC and Merck: wear light, loose-fitting clothing.
